justice: The roadway is generously dimensioned with multiple lanes, medians, and wide paved edges, showing substantial space allocation, but most visible space is devoted to motor traffic rather than to clearly usable pedestrian areas.

A sidewalk is visible on the right side and another paved edge appears on the left, which suggests some provision for non-drivers, yet there is no clearly marked dedicated cycling facility visible in the scene.
Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free details are clearly visible at the intersection or along the sidewalks from this image.
safety: The road surface is new and smooth, and the lane arrows and lane markings are highly legible, which helps all road users understand movements at the intersection.
A central metal barrier separates opposing directions and reduces risky mid-block conflicts, improving traffic safety for drivers and helping organize movement.
The intersection ahead includes a marked crosswalk and traffic signals, which generally support safer crossing control, although the very wide carriageway still creates a long crossing distance.
livability: The street appears to run through a low-activity area with open land, sparse roadside uses, and no visible shops, services, or active frontages that would support daily street life.
There are no visible benches, bus stops, kiosks, or gathering spaces, so the corridor functions mainly as a movement space rather than a socially vibrant place.
The broad setbacks, empty sidewalks, and absence of visible pedestrians or cyclists make the environment feel less lively and less supportive of everyday public life.
sustainability: Street trees and planted medians are present, which adds some green infrastructure and can contribute to long-term environmental performance.
However, the corridor is dominated by wide asphalt carriageways and turning lanes, indicating a strong car-oriented layout with high land consumption for vehicle movement.
No dedicated bike lane, bus priority feature, or visible transit stop is evident in the image, limiting support for lower-carbon travel modes.
aesthetics: The street has a clean, orderly appearance with fresh asphalt, crisp white lane markings, and neatly maintained medians and sidewalks.
The mountain backdrop and open sky create a strong visual setting that improves scenic quality beyond the roadway itself.
Young street trees and trimmed planting strips provide some visual softness, although the overall scene still feels sparse and infrastructural rather than richly detailed.
comfort: Thermal comfort appears limited because the trees are young and provide very little shade over the sidewalks or roadway.
Physical comfort is mixed: the asphalt and paved edges look smooth and even, but no seating, shelter, or resting facilities are visible for people spending time on the street.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the very wide road geometry and large turning space, which can make the environment feel exposed and vehicle-dominated for non-motorized users.
walkability: Sidewalks are present on both sides or edges of the corridor, which supports basic pedestrian continuity along the street.
Walkability is weakened by the large width of the intersection and multiple traffic lanes, creating a long and potentially tiring crossing for pedestrians even though a crosswalk is marked ahead.

There is little shade, no visible seating, and no active frontage along the sidewalks, so the route appears functional for walking but not especially inviting or comfortable for everyday pedestrian use.
